opus-5.5.text:
Sure. The core idea is actually pretty intuitive once you look at how people really use large language models today.

When you run an LLM, for every token it processes it computes what we call the KV cache, the key and value tensors from the attention layers. That's expensive to compute, and traditionally, inference engines throw it away as soon as a request finishes. But if you look at real workloads, there's a huge amount of shared prefix across requests. You have the same long system prompt sent over and over, few-shot examples reused in every call, multi-turn chat where each new turn contains the entire previous conversation, agents that branch out from the same context, tree-of-thought search, and so on. Recomputing all of that every time is just wasted GPU work.

So RadixAttention says: let's keep the KV cache around after a request finishes, and organize it so we can find and reuse matching prefixes automatically. The data structure we use is a radix tree. Each edge in the tree is labeled with a sequence of tokens, and the nodes hold the corresponding KV cache tensors. When a new request comes in, we walk down the tree to find the longest prefix that's already been computed, reuse that part directly, and only compute the new tokens. Then we insert the new part back into the tree, so the next request can benefit from it too.

Of course, GPU memory is limited, so you can't keep everything forever. We use an LRU eviction policy, evicting leaf nodes first, so the most commonly shared prefixes, which sit near the root, tend to stay. And we pair that with a cache-aware scheduling policy: instead of serving requests strictly first-come-first-served, we prioritize requests with longer matched prefixes, which raises the cache hit rate a lot. In our experiments, that ordering got pretty close to the optimal hit rate.

What I like about the design is that it's automatic. Developers don't have to manually tell the system "please cache this prompt." You just write your program, whether it's a chatbot, an agent, or a complicated multi-call pipeline, and the runtime discovers the sharing on its own. That's a big part of why we saw substantial throughput improvements, in some workloads up to several times faster, on the kinds of structured, multi-call LLM programs that are becoming really common.

r001.rationale: The response says a new request reuses the KV cache for its longest already-computed prefix and computes only the new tokens.

r002.rationale: It states that RadixAttention uses a radix tree whose token-labeled edges index prefixes.

r003.rationale: It says tree nodes hold corresponding KV cache tensors, but does not state that the cache is stored in a memory pool.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The core idea is actually pretty simple once you see what's being wasted in a typical LLM serving system.

When you run a model like a chatbot, every request comes in with a prompt, and before the model can generate anything it has to process that prompt and build up what we call the KV cache, the key-value tensors for every token. That's the expensive part, especially for long prompts. In most serving systems, once a request finishes, that cache gets thrown away. The next request comes in, and even if the first ninety percent of the prompt is identical, you recompute all of it from scratch.

And if you look at real workloads, that overlap is everywhere. Multiple turns of a chat all share the same system prompt and conversation history. Few-shot prompting repeats the same examples across hundreds of calls. Agent workflows, tree search, self-consistency, these all branch off from a shared prefix. So we're constantly recomputing the same thing.

RadixAttention is just the observation that you should keep that KV cache around and share it automatically. The way we do it is with a radix tree, which is a kind of compressed prefix tree. Every path from the root corresponds to a token sequence, and the nodes store the KV cache for those tokens. When a new request arrives, you walk down the tree, match the longest prefix that's already there, and only compute the tokens that are new. If two requests share a prefix, they literally point at the same cache entries.

The tree structure matters because sharing isn't just one level deep. You might have a system prompt, then several different conversation histories branching from it, then different latest messages branching from each of those. A radix tree captures that whole hierarchy naturally, and it supports insertion, lookup, and splitting nodes when a new request diverges partway through.

The other piece is eviction. GPU memory is limited, so you can't keep everything forever. We use an LRU policy on the leaves, which fits well because a leaf that hasn't been touched recently is the least likely to be useful, and you never evict a node that's still a prefix of something active.

And then one more thing that makes it work well in practice is cache-aware scheduling. If you reorder the requests in your queue so the ones that share prefixes run close together, your hit rate goes way up. So the runtime isn't just passively caching, it's actively arranging the work to exploit the sharing.

The nice part is that it's completely automatic. The user doesn't annotate anything or decide what to cache. You just write your program and the runtime finds the reuse for you. In the workloads we looked at, that translated into throughput improvements of several times over systems that didn't do this.

r001.rationale: It says a new request matches the longest existing prefix and reuses its KV cache, computing only new tokens.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes RadixAttention using a radix tree, a compressed prefix tree, to represent token-sequence prefixes.

r003.rationale: It says tree nodes store KV cache, but does not state that the cache is stored in a memory pool.

astra-6.text:
The core idea is to reuse computation when different requests share the same prompt prefix. When a language model processes a prompt, it produces intermediate states called the key-value, or KV, cache. If another request starts with the same tokens, we can reuse those states instead of computing them again.

RadixAttention organizes that cache in a radix tree, which is a compact prefix tree. Requests with a common beginning share the same branch, and when their tokens diverge, they split into different branches. That lets us efficiently find the longest cached prefix for a new request and compute only the part that’s new.

For example, you might have many requests using the same system prompt and few-shot examples, or several generations branching from the same conversation. Those can all benefit from prefix reuse. As memory fills up, we evict less recently used cached portions.

The important part is that SGLang manages this reuse automatically across requests, so applications can benefit without manually managing the KV cache.

r001.rationale: It says requests with the same starting tokens can reuse the KV states already computed for that prefix.

r002.rationale: It describes RadixAttention organizing the cache in a radix tree, with shared branches for common beginnings and splits where tokens diverge.

r003.rationale: It discusses organizing and evicting cached portions, but does not state that the prefix index maps to computed KV cache stored in a memory pool.

sol-6.1.text:
The core idea is to reuse computation whenever requests share the same prefix. In an LLM, processing a prompt produces key-value states, or the KV cache. If another request starts with the same tokens, we can reuse those states instead of computing them again.

RadixAttention organizes that cache in a radix tree. Shared token prefixes share a path in the tree, and requests branch where their tokens diverge. When a new request comes in, we find the longest prefix already cached and compute only the remaining part.

That’s especially useful for workloads with repeated system prompts, few-shot examples, or multiple calls that branch from the same conversation. SGLang manages the reuse automatically, keeping useful cached prefixes and evicting them when memory is needed. So the main benefit is less redundant computation and higher throughput.

r001.rationale: It says requests with the same token prefix can reuse the already computed KV states instead of recomputing them.

r002.rationale: It explains that RadixAttention organizes cached prefixes in a radix tree, where shared prefixes share a path and requests branch at divergences.

r003.rationale: It connects the tree to cached KV states, but does not state that those states are stored in a memory pool or that the prefix index maps to such a pool.
